questions.q: Which one of the following graphs is not applicable for a 1st order reaction (R $\rightarrow$ P)?
options: A graph of [R] vs t with a downward sloping curve.
A graph of ln[R] vs t with a downward sloping straight line.
A graph of log$_{10}$[R] vs t with an upward sloping straight line.
A graph of log$_{10}$([R]$_0$/[R]) vs t with an upward sloping straight line through the origin.
questions.note: The standard answer is (C): log$_{10}$[R] vs t must slope downward for a first-order reaction, so that graph (upward-sloping) is the one that is not applicable; option (A), [R] vs t as a downward curve, is a correct first-order graph, not the exception.
questions.explanation: For a first-order reaction, log$_{10}$[R] decreases linearly with time (downward sloping), not upward, so option (C) is the description that is not applicable; KEA's key for this version instead marks option (A) — the key's answer is retained here (as per KEA key).

questions.q: For a reaction having three steps, the overall rate constant is K = $\dfrac{k_1k_3}{k_2}$. The values of E$_{a1}$, E$_{a2}$, and E$_{a3}$ (activation energies stepwise) are 40, 50 and 60 kJ mol$^{-1}$ respectively. Then the overall E$_a$ (activation energy) of the reaction is
questions.note: The standard answer is (C) 50 kJ mol$^{-1}$, from $E_a = E_{a1}+E_{a3}-E_{a2} = 40+60-50$; option (A) 30 kJ mol$^{-1}$ does not follow from the given activation energies.
questions.explanation: Since $K=k_1k_3/k_2$, the Arrhenius exponents add as $E_a = E_{a1}+E_{a3}-E_{a2} = 40+60-50 = 50$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ (option C); KEA's key for this version instead marks option (A) — the key's answer is retained here (as per KEA key).

questions.q: For a 1st order change R $\rightarrow$ P, the concentration of Reactant R changes from 0.1 M to 0.025 M in 40 minutes. The rate of reaction when the concentration of R is 0.01 M is
The activation energy for the reaction X $\rightarrow$ Y is 150 kJ mol$^{-1}$. The change in enthalpy for the above reaction is -135 kJ mol$^{-1}$. Then the activation energy for Y $\rightarrow$ X is
questions.explanation: E$_a$(reverse) = E$_a$(forward) - $\Delta H$ = 150 - (-135) = 285 kJ mol$^{-1}$.

questions.q: Catalysts are used to increase the rate of a chemical reaction. Because it
options: Increases the activation energy of the reaction
Decreases the activation energy of the reaction
Brings about improper orientation of reactant molecules
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, thereby increasing the rate of reaction.

questions.q: Half-life of a first order reaction is 20 seconds and initial concentration of reactant is 0.2M. The concentration of reactant left after 80 seconds is
questions.explanation: 80 seconds corresponds to 80/20 = 4 half-lives, so the concentration remaining is 0.2/2$^4$ = 0.0125 M.

questions.q: In the given graph [potential energy vs reaction coordinate, showing activation energy E$_a$=215 kJ for the forward reaction and $\Delta H$=90 kJ, an exothermic reaction with products lower in energy than reactants], E$_a$ for the reverse reaction will be
questions.explanation: Since the reaction is exothermic with $\Delta H = 90$ kJ, $E_a(\text{reverse}) = E_a(\text{forward}) - \Delta H = 215 - 90 = 125$ kJ.

questions.q: For the reaction 2N$_2$O$_5$(g) $\rightarrow$ 4NO$_2$(g) + O$_2$(g), initial concentration of N$_2$O$_5$ is 2.0 mol L$^{-1}$ and after 300 min, it is reduced to 1.4 mol L$^{-1}$. The rate of production of NO$_2$ (in mol L$^{-1}$min$^{-1}$) is
questions.explanation: Rate of consumption of N$_2$O$_5$ = (2.0-1.4)/300 = 2×10$^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$min$^{-1}$; since NO$_2$ forms at twice the rate of N$_2$O$_5$ consumption (from stoichiometry), rate of production of NO$_2$ = 2×(2×10$^{-3}$) = 4×10$^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$min$^{-1}$.

questions.q: For the reaction A $\rightleftharpoons$ B, E$_a$ = 50 kJ mol$^{-1}$ and $\Delta H$ = -20 kJ mol$^{-1}$. When a catalyst is added, E$_a$ decreases by 10 kJ mol$^{-1}$. What is the E$_a$ for the backward reaction in the presence of catalyst?
questions.explanation: $\Delta H = (E_a)_f - (E_a)_b$; with the catalyst $(E_a)_f = 40$, so $-20 = 40 - (E_a)_b$, giving $(E_a)_b = 60$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.

questions.q: For the reaction PCl$_5$ $\rightarrow$ PCl$_3$ + Cl$_2$, rate and rate constant are $1.02\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$ and $3.4\times10^{-5}$s$^{-1}$ respectively at a given instant. The molar concentration of PCl$_5$ at that instant is:
Which one of the following does not represent Arrhenius equation?
questions.explanation: The Arrhenius equation has a negative exponent, $k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$; option D has the sign reversed and so does not represent it.

questions.q: In which one of the following reactions, rate constant has the unit mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ ?
options: Decomposition of HI on the surface of Gold
questions.explanation: Rate constant units of mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ correspond to a zero-order reaction; the surface-catalysed decomposition of HI on gold is zero order because the metal surface is saturated, while the other reactions are pseudo-first, three-halves and third order respectively.

questions.q: For a reaction, the value of rate constant at 300 K is 6.0 $\times$ 10$^5$ s$^{-1}$. The value of Arrhenius factor A at infinitely high temperature is :
questions.explanation: As T $\to \infty$, $Ea/RT \to 0$, so $k=Ae^0=A$: the Arrhenius factor A is just the rate constant in the infinite-temperature limit. Since Ea isn't given, options depending on it can't be evaluated, leaving A = 6 $\times$ 10$^5$ s$^{-1}$ as the only determinable answer.

questions.q: The rate constants k$_1$ and k$_2$ for two different reactions are 10$^{16}$ $\times$ e$^{-2000/T}$ and 10$^{15}$ $\times$ e$^{-1000/T}$ respectively. The temperature at which k$_1$ = k$_2$ is :
A first order reaction is half completed in 45 min. How long does it need 99.9% of the reaction to be completed?
questions.explanation: t$_{1/2}$ = 45 min gives k = 0.693/45 min$^{-1}$. Time for 99.9% completion = (2.303/k) log(100/0.1) = (2.303 $\times$ 45/0.693) $\times$ 3 $\approx$ 449 min $\approx$ 7.5 hours.

questions.q: The rate of the reaction: CH$_3$COOC$_2$H$_5$ + NaOH $\rightarrow$ CH$_3$COONa + C$_2$H$_5$OH is given by the equation, Rate = K[CH$_3$COOC$_2$H$_5$][NaOH]. If concentration is expressed in mol L$^{-1}$, the unit of K is
questions.explanation: This is an overall second order reaction, so k has units of (mol L$^{-1}$)$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ = L mol$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$.

questions.q: For n$^{th}$ order of reaction, Half-life period is directly proportional to
questions.explanation: For an n$^{th}$ order reaction, t$_{1/2}$ $\propto$ a$^{1-n}$, where a is the initial concentration.

questions.q: Half-life of a reaction is found to be inversely proportional to the fifth power of its initial concentration, the order of reaction is

For a reaction A + 2B → Products, when concentration of B alone is increased half life remains the same. If concentration of A alone is doubled, rate remains the same. The unit of rate constant for the reaction is
questions.explanation: Half-life independent of concentration of B means order in B is 1; rate unchanged when [A] is doubled means order in A is 0. Overall order = 1, so rate constant unit is s$^{-1}$.

questions.q: If the rate constant for a first order reaction is k, the time (t) required for the completion of 99% of the reaction is given by
The rate of a gaseous reaction is given by the expression k[A][B]$^2$. If the volume of vessel is reduced to one half of the initial volume, the reaction rate as compared to original rate is
questions.explanation: Halving volume doubles all concentrations. New rate = k(2A)(2B)$^2$ = 8 × (original rate).

questions.q: Higher order ( > 3) reactions are rare due to
options: Shifting of equilibrium towards reactants due to elastic collisions
Loss of active species on collision
Low probability of simultaneous collision of all reacting species
Increase in entropy as more molecules are involved
questions.explanation: The probability that more than three molecules collide simultaneously with correct orientation and energy is extremely low, making higher order reactions rare.

questions.q: The time required for 60% completion of a first order reaction is 50 min. The time required for 93.6% completion of the same reaction will be
questions.explanation: $t\propto\log\dfrac{100}{100-x}$; ratio of times = $\log(100/6.4)/\log(100/40) = \log15.625/\log2.5 = 3$, so t$_2$ = 3$\times$50 = 150 min.

questions.q: For an elementary reaction 2A + 3B $\to$ 4C + D the rate of appearance of C at time 't' is 2.8 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$S$^{-1}$. Rate of disappearance of B at 't' will be
questions.explanation: Rate $= \dfrac14\dfrac{d[C]}{dt} = \dfrac13\left(-\dfrac{d[B]}{dt}\right)$, so $-\dfrac{d[B]}{dt} = \dfrac34\times\dfrac{d[C]}{dt} = \dfrac34(2.8\times10^{-3})$.

questions.q: The rate constant of a reaction is given by k = PZe$^{-Ea/RT}$ under standard notation. In order to speed up the reaction, which of the following factors has to be decreased?
questions.explanation: Rate constant increases as the activation energy E$_a$ decreases (it appears with a negative sign in the exponent).

questions.q: Which is a wrong statement?
options: Rate constant k = Arrhenius constant A, if Ea = 0
ln k vs $\dfrac{1}{T}$ plot is a straight line.
e$^{-Ea/RT}$ gives the fraction of reactant molecules that are activated at the given temp
presence of catalyst will not alter the value of Ea
questions.explanation: A catalyst works precisely by lowering the activation energy Ea, so the statement that a catalyst does not alter Ea is wrong.

questions.q: 1 L of 2 M CH$_3$COOH is mixed with 1 L of 3M C$_2$H$_5$OH to form an ester. The rate of the reaction with respect to the initial rate when each solution is diluted with an equal volume of water will be
questions.explanation: Esterification rate $\propto$ [acid][alcohol]; diluting each solution with an equal volume of water halves both concentrations, so the new rate is $(1/2)\times(1/2)=1/4=0.25$ times the initial rate.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of homogeneous catalysis?
options: oxidation of NH$_3$ in Ostwald's process
oxidation of SO$_2$ in lead chamber process
oxidation of SO$_2$ in contact process
manufacture of NH$_3$ by Haber's process
questions.explanation: In the lead chamber process, NO gas catalyses the oxidation of SO2 while remaining in the same (gas) phase as the reactants, making it homogeneous catalysis; the other three use solid catalysts with gaseous reactants (heterogeneous).

questions.q: The plot of t$_{1/2}$ v/s [R]$_0$ for a reaction is a straight-line parallel to x-axis. The unit for the rate constant of this reaction is
questions.explanation: t1/2 independent of initial concentration ([R]0) is the hallmark of a first-order reaction, whose rate constant has units of s$^{-1}$.

questions.q: For the reaction, 2SO$_2$ + O$_2$ $\rightleftharpoons$ 2SO$_3$, the rate of disappearance of O$_2$ is 2$\times$10$^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$. The rate of appearance of SO$_3$ is
questions.explanation: Since 2 mol SO$_3$ forms per 1 mol O$_2$ consumed, rate of SO$_3$ formation = 2 $\times$ (rate of O$_2$ disappearance) = 4$\times$10$^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$.

questions.q: The temperature coefficient of a reaction is 2. When the temperature is increased from 30$^\circ$C to 90$^\circ$C, the rate of reaction is increased by
questions.explanation: A 60$^\circ$C rise equals six 10$^\circ$C intervals; rate increases by (temperature coefficient)$^6$ = 2$^6$ = 64 times.

questions.q: The value of rate constant of a pseudo first order reaction
options: Depends on the concentration of reactants present in small amounts
Depends on the concentration of reactants present in excess
Is independent of the concentration of reactants
questions.explanation: In a pseudo first order reaction, the reactant present in large excess has its concentration folded into the rate constant, so the rate 'constant' depends on the concentration of that excess reactant.

questions.q: Which of the following statement is in accordance with the Arrhenius equation ?
options: Rate of a reaction increases with increase in temperature
Rate of a reaction increases with decrease in activation energy
Rate constant decreases exponentially with increase in temperature
Rate of reaction does not change with increase in activation energy
questions.explanation: By the Arrhenius equation $k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$, the rate constant (and hence rate) increases both with increasing temperature and with decreasing activation energy, so statements A and B are both correct.

questions.q: Which of the following statement is incorrect ?
options: The rate law for any reaction cannot be determined experimentally
Biomolecular reactions involve simultaneous collision between two species
Molecularity is only applicable for elementary reaction.
questions.explanation: Rate laws are in fact determined experimentally (e.g. by the method of initial rates), so statement A is the incorrect one.

questions.q: For a reaction $\dfrac{1}{2}$A $\rightarrow$ 2B rate of disappearance of A is related to rate of appearance of B by the expression
questions.explanation: For $\dfrac{1}{2}$A$\to$2B, rate $=-\dfrac{1}{1/2}\dfrac{d[A]}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[B]}{dt}$, which simplifies to $-\dfrac{d[A]}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{d[B]}{dt}$.

questions.q: The half-life period of a 1st order reaction is 60 minutes. What percentage will be left over after 240 minutes ?
questions.explanation: 240 minutes = 4 half-lives, so fraction remaining = (1/2)$^4$ = 1/16 = 6.25%.

questions.q: For a chemical reaction, mA $\rightarrow$ xB, the rate law is r = k[A]$^2$. If the concentration of A is doubled, the reaction rate will be,
questions.explanation: Since rate $\propto$ [A]$^2$, doubling [A] increases rate by 2$^2$ = 4 times (quadrupled).

questions.q: 3A $\longrightarrow$ 2B, rate of reaction $+\dfrac{d[B]}{dt}$ is equal to
questions.explanation: Rate $= -\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[A]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[B]}{dt}$, so $\dfrac{d[B]}{dt} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\dfrac{d[A]}{dt}$.

questions.q: The activation energy of a chemical reaction can be determined by,
options: evaluating rate constants at two different temperatures.
evaluating the concentration of reactants at two different temperatures.
evaluating rate constant at standard temperature.
questions.explanation: Using the Arrhenius equation, activation energy is found from rate constants measured at two different temperatures (KEA key also accepted option 4).

questions.q: In a first order reaction, the concentration of the reactant is reduced to 12.5% in one hour. When was it half completed?
questions.explanation: 12.5% remaining = 1/8 = (1/2)$^3$, i.e. 3 half-lives occur in 60 minutes, so one half-life = 20 minutes.

questions.q: Half life period of a first order reaction is 10 min. Starting with initial concentration 12 M, the rate after 20 min is
questions.explanation: k = 0.693/10 = 0.0693 min$^{-1}$; after 20 min (2 half-lives) concentration falls from 12 M to 3 M, so rate = k[A] = 0.0693 $\times$ 3 M min$^{-1}$.

questions.q: 100 cm$^3$ of 1 M CH$_3$COOH was mixed with 100 cm$^3$ of 2 M CH$_3$OH to form an ester. The change in the initial rate if each solution is diluted with equal volume of water would be
questions.explanation: Esterification is second order overall, rate = k[acid][alcohol]; diluting both reactants to half their concentration reduces the rate to (1/2)$\times$(1/2) = 0.25 times the original.

questions.q: A$_{(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} P_{(g)} + Q_{(g)} + R_{(g)}$, follows first order kinetics with a half life of 69.3 s at 500 °C. Starting from the gas 'A' enclosed in a container at 500 °C and at a pressure of 0.4 atm, the total pressure of the system after 230 s will be
questions.explanation: k = ln2/69.3 = 0.01 s$^{-1}$; kt = 0.01×230 = 2.3, so fraction remaining = e$^{-2.3}$ ≈ 0.1, i.e. x = 0.9×0.4 = 0.36 atm decomposed. Since 1 mol A gives 3 mol products, total pressure = 0.4 + 2x = 0.4 + 0.72 = 1.12 atm.

questions.q:
A plot of $\dfrac{1}{T}$ Vs. ln k for a reaction gives the slope –1 × 10$^4$ K. The energy of activation for the reaction is

(Given R = 8.314 J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: From the Arrhenius equation, slope = -E$_a$/R, so E$_a$ = -slope×R = 1×10$^4$×8.314 = 83140 J/mol = 83.14 kJ/mol. KEA awarded a grace mark for this question.

questions.q: If 50% of the reactant is converted into a product in a first order reaction in 25 minutes, how much of it would react in 100 minutes ?
questions.explanation: Half-life = 25 min, so 100 min = 4 half-lives; fraction remaining = (1/2)$^4$ = 1/16, so 93.75% has reacted.

questions.q: The rate of reaction increases with rise in temperature because of
options: increase in number of activated molecules.
increase in the number of effective collisions.
questions.explanation: Raising temperature increases the number of molecules with energy above the activation energy, which also increases the number of effective collisions; the KEA key accepts both (1) and (4).

questions.q: Temperature coefficient of a reaction is '2'. When temperature is increased from 30 °C to 90 °C, the rate of reaction is increased by
questions.explanation: A rise of 60 °C is six 10 °C intervals; rate increases by 2$^6$ = 64 times.

questions.q: For a reaction: A + B → Products, the rate of the reaction at various concentrations are given below: [table: Expt1 A=0.2,B=0.2,rate=2; Expt2 A=0.2,B=0.4,rate=4; Expt3 A=0.6,B=0.4,rate=36] The rate law for the above reaction is
questions.explanation: Comparing expts 1 & 2 (A constant, B doubles, rate doubles): order in B = 1. Comparing expts 2 & 3 (B constant, A triples, rate increases 9×): order in A = 2. Rate law: r=K[A]$^2$[B].

questions.q: A first order reaction is 60% complete in 20 minutes. How long will the reaction take to be 84% complete?
questions.explanation: $k=\dfrac{2.303}{20}\log\dfrac{100}{40}$. For 84% completion, $t=\dfrac{2.303}{k}\log\dfrac{100}{16}$. Since $100/16=(100/40)^2$ approx, $t\approx2\times20=40$ minutes.

questions.q: A given sample of milk turns sour at room temperature (27 °C) in 5 hours. In a refrigerator at −3 °C, it can be stored 10 times longer. The energy of activation for the souring of milk is
questions.explanation: $T_1=270K, T_2=300K$, $k_2/k_1=10$ (10× longer at lower temperature means 10× slower rate). $\ln(k_2/k_1)=\dfrac{E_a}{R}\dfrac{T_2-T_1}{T_1T_2}\Rightarrow2.303=\dfrac{E_a}{R}\times\dfrac{30}{270\times300}$, giving $E_a=2.303\times2700R$ J/mol $=2.303\times2.7R$ kJ/mol.

questions.q: At 300 K, a gaseous reaction: A → B + C was found to follow first order kinetics. Starting with pure A, the total pressure at the end of 20 minutes was 100 mm of Hg. The total pressure after the completion of the reaction is 180 mm of Hg. The partial pressure of A (in mm of Hg) is
questions.explanation: Initial pressure of A, $P_0=90$ mm (since total pressure doubles to 180 as A fully decomposes to B+C). At t=20 min, $P_t=P_0+x=100$, so $x=10$; partial pressure of A remaining $=P_0-x=90-10=80$ mm.

questions.q:
The following data were obtained during the first order decomposition of $2A_{(g)} \rightarrow B_{(g)}+C_{(s)}$ at a constant volume and at a particular temperature.
At the end of 10 min, total pressure = 300 Pascal.
After completion, total pressure = 200 Pascal.
The rate constant in min$^{-1}$ is ..............
questions.explanation: Since C is solid, total pressure $=P_0-p$ where $p$ is the pressure of B formed; at completion $P_0/2=200\Rightarrow P_0=400$ Pa, so at 10 min $P_A=200$ Pa; $k=\dfrac{2.303}{10}\log\dfrac{400}{200}=0.0693\\ min^{-1}$.

questions.q: The time required for 100% completion of a zero order reaction is ..............
questions.explanation: For a zero order reaction, $[A]=a-kt$; complete consumption occurs when $t=a/k$.

questions.q: The activation energy of a reaction at a given temperature is found to be 2.303 RT J mol$^{-1}$. The ratio of rate constant to the Arrhenius factor is ..............
The activation energy for a reaction at the temperature TK was found to be 2.303 RT J mol$^{-1}$. The ratio of the rate constant to Arrhenius factor is ...............
Time required for 100 percent completion of a zero order reaction is ...............
questions.explanation: For a zero order reaction, $kt = x$; complete reaction means $x = a$, so $t = a/k$.

questions.q:
The following data is obtained during the first order thermal decomposition of $2A_{(g)} \longrightarrow B_{(g)} + C_{(s)}$, at constant volume and temperature.

[Table: At the end of 10 minutes, total pressure = 300 Pa; After completion, total pressure = 200 Pa]

The rate constant in min$^{-1}$ is ...............
questions.explanation: Total pressure at completion = $P_0/2 = 200$ Pa, so $P_0 = 400$ Pa; at t=10 min, pressure of A left = $2(P_0 - 300) = 200$ Pa. $k = \dfrac{2.303}{10}\log\dfrac{400}{200} = 0.0693\ min^{-1}$.

questions.q: Which one of the following is an example for homogeneous catalysis?
options: Manufacture of ammonia by Haber's process
Manufacture of sulphuric acid by contact process
Hydrolysis of sucrose in presence of dilute hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: In acid hydrolysis of sucrose, the HCl catalyst and the sucrose solution are in the same (liquid) phase, making it homogeneous catalysis, unlike the other options which use solid catalysts with gaseous/liquid reactants.

questions.q: For a chemical reaction A $\to$ B, the rate of the reaction is $2 \times 10^{-3}$ mol dm$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$, when the initial concentration is 0.05 mol dm$^{-3}$. The rate of the same reaction is $1.6 \times 10^{-2}$ mol dm$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$ when the initial concentration is 0.1 mol dm$^{-3}$. The order of the reaction is
questions.explanation: Rate increases 8-fold when concentration doubles: $2^n=8 \Rightarrow n=3$.

questions.q: For the decomposition of a compound AB at 600 K, the following data were obtained: [AB] 0.20, 0.40, 0.60 mol dm$^{-3}$ give rates $2.75\times10^{-8}$, $11.0\times10^{-8}$, $24.75\times10^{-8}$ mol dm$^{-3}$s$^{-1}$ respectively. The order for the decomposition of AB is
questions.explanation: Doubling [AB] quadruples the rate ($11.0/2.75=4=2^2$), so the order is 2.

questions.q: The rate equation for a reaction : A $\to$ B is r = K[A]$^0$. If the initial concentration of the reactant is a mol dm$^{-3}$, the half life period of the reaction is
questions.explanation: For a zero-order reaction, $t_{1/2} = a/(2K)$.
